It sounds simple, yet the New Jersey manual spends real care on it, because hand position affects both control and safety when an air bag goes off. We will cover where your hands belong for normal driving, the one grip you must never use, when a hand may leave the wheel, how firmly to hold it, and where to keep the car in its lane. Then we move to hand-over-hand steering: how far the hands travel, how a turn starts, how you straighten out, and where the method works best.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The nine and three grip","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Outside rim at nine and three.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]},{"text":"Thumbs rest along the face.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]},{"text":"Lowers air bag injury risk.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"For normal driving, hold the outside rim of the steering wheel at the nine and three o'clock positions, with your thumbs resting along the face of the wheel. Picture the wheel as a clock: your left hand sits where the nine would be and your right hand where the three would be. This is not only about comfort. Holding the wheel at those positions lowers the risk of hand, wrist or arm injury if the air bag deploys. So the grip that gives you good control is also the grip that protects your arms.
